08-010.r: Sound cannot travel in vacuum: it is a mechanical wave needing a medium (solid, liquid or gas); light, heat and electromagnetic waves can cross vacuum.

08-011.r: Radio waves are electromagnetic (R true), so they are generally unaffected by magnetic and electric fields; they do not bend in a magnetic field (A false).

08-012.r: Cosmic rays → very high-energy charged particles moving near light speed, from the Sun or outside the solar system; they are not electromagnetic waves.

08-014.r: Radiation needs no medium (radio waves, microwaves, infrared, light, X-rays, gamma rays); conduction and convection need a medium.

08-015.r: Albedo → reflecting power: fraction of light reflected by a surface; fresh snow up to 95% (0.95), water as low as 3% (0.03).

08-016.r: Statement-I false: atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial (long-wave) radiation than by incoming solar radiation. Statement-II true: CO2 and greenhouse gases absorb long-wave radiation well.

08-017.r: Atmosphere is heated mainly by long-wave terrestrial radiation; short-wave insolation heats Earth's surface (about 51% absorbed), which then radiates heat to the air.
08-017.h: Sun heats the ground, the ground heats the air.

08-019.r: Clouds and gases reflect about one-fourth of incoming solar radiation (true); Earth's surface re-emits heat as infrared, not ultraviolet (false).
08-019.t: Don't confuse: Earth re-emits infrared (long-wave) radiation, not ultraviolet.

08-020.r: True: heat trapped by the atmosphere keeps Earth's average temperature; CO2-like gases trap radiation well. False: no atmosphere → below freezing everywhere (only the average, about –18°C).

08-021.r: Distance between two successive crests or two successive troughs → wavelength.

08-022.r: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum, about 3 lakh km per second (option a).

08-023.r: X-rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves → not deflected by electric or magnetic fields; they can be diffracted or scattered by matter (basis of X-ray diffraction).

08-024.r: Supersonic waves are not electromagnetic (supersonic = faster than sound); gamma rays, X-rays and ultraviolet rays are electromagnetic waves.
08-024.c: The book's explanation says γ-rays, X-rays and UV rays are 'examples of supersonic waves'; it means electromagnetic waves. The answer (d) is right.

08-025.r: Longest wavelength → radio waves. Order: radio > microwave > infrared > visible > ultraviolet > X-rays > gamma rays (shortest).
08-025.h: Radio to gamma: "Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns"; wavelength falls along it.

08-026.r: Shorter wavelength → higher frequency and energy. Energy: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < UV < X-rays < gamma; among options X-rays have maximum energy.

08-027.r: Decreasing frequency: gamma rays > X-rays > ultraviolet > radio waves (code 1, 4, 2, 3).

08-028.r: Increasing frequency: radio waves < infrared < visible < X-rays (IV, III, II, I).

08-029.r: Microwaves → wavelength about 1 m to 1 mm, frequency about 300 MHz–300 GHz; best option: 1 GHz–300 GHz.

08-030.r: Crystal structure is found with X-rays (X-ray diffraction); crystallography also uses neutron and electron diffraction.

08-031.r: Radar uses radio waves to find the range, angle or velocity of objects such as enemy aircraft, ships and vehicles.

08-032.r: Remote sensing uses electromagnetic waves: it records electromagnetic energy reflected or emitted by Earth's surface, usually from a satellite or aircraft.

08-033.r: Ozone depletion lets more ultraviolet reach Earth; UV wavelength is about 10⁻⁷ m (UV-A 320–400 nm; UV-B 280–320 nm, mostly absorbed by ozone).

08-034.r: Night vision apparatus uses infrared waves (longer wavelength than visible light); soldiers use it to find targets and intruders at night.

08-035.r: TV remote control uses infrared rays (infrared electromagnetic radiation).
08-035.t: Remote → infrared; if infrared is not an option, choose radio waves (some remotes use them).

08-038.r: TV remote control: most use infrared waves, some use radio waves; with no infrared option, answer radio waves.
08-038.t: Don't pick microwaves or sound waves; both infrared and radio waves are electromagnetic.

08-039.r: Telecommunication → microwaves (300 MHz–300 GHz): carry thousands of channels; used for point-to-point links, terrestrial relays and satellite communication.

08-040.r: Superimposing information (audio or video) on carrier radio waves → modulation.

08-041.r: Not true: 'FM's frequency range is lower than AM's'. FM was invented by Edwin Armstrong (paper 1935) and needs wider bandwidth than AM.

08-042.r: FM suits medium-speed communication of 1200–2400 bits per second; FM broadcast band 88–108 MHz; AM radio 530–1710 kHz (max 1200 bits per second).

08-044.r: Frequency = speed of light ÷ wavelength (ν = c/λ): 3 × 10⁸ m/s ÷ 30 m = 10 MHz.
08-044.h: Use c = ν × λ: divide light speed by wavelength.

08-045.r: Ionosphere helps radio communication because of its electrically charged ions, not ozone; long wavelength of radio waves is not the reason (neither statement accepted).

08-046.r: Dish TV fails in rain: raindrops absorb radio-wave energy (turning it to heat) and scatter it from its direction; weak signals miss small antennas (all three correct).

08-047.r: X-rays (electromagnetic radiation) are used to diagnose intestinal diseases.
08-047.t: Don't confuse X-rays with α, β, γ rays from radioactive decay.

08-048.r: CT scan (computed tomography) → X-rays plus a computer give cross-sectional images of the body.

08-049.r: X-rays (X-ray machine) → discovered by Wilhelm Rontgen; wavelength about 0.01 to 10 nanometres; used in medicine and industry.

09-001.r: Speed of sound, ascending: nitrogen (gas) < water (liquid) < steel (solid) → III, I, II.

09-002.r: Sound is fastest in solids (steel/metal), slower in liquids, slowest in gases; in air about 330 m/s (344 m/s at 22°C); iron 5950 m/s.
09-002.h: Solid > Liquid > Gas: tighter particles, faster sound.

09-005.r: Speed of sound: air < water < steel (Va < Vw < Vs).

09-006.r: At about 20°C, sound is fastest in iron (among air, granite, water, iron); speed depends on elasticity and density of the medium.

09-007.r: Speed of sound at 25°C: air 346 m/s, hydrogen 1284 m/s, water 1498 m/s, steel 5960 m/s → fastest in steel.

09-008.r: Sound waves travel through solids, liquids and gases (fastest in solids), but not through vacuum.

09-009.r: Sound (a mechanical wave) is fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases; it cannot travel through vacuum.

09-012.r: Walls of a music concert hall should absorb sound (soft surfaces) so that reflected sound does not create echoes.

09-013.r: Echo → reflection of sound from a hard, flat surface back to the listener.

09-014.r: Clear echo → minimum distance about 16.5 m (about 17 m) between the observer/sound source and the reflecting surface.

09-016.r: Speed = frequency × wavelength = 4 kHz × 0.35 m = 1.4 km/s; time for 3 km = 3 ÷ 1.4 ≈ 2.14 s.

09-017.r: Pitch depends on frequency: high pitch = high frequency; low pitch = low frequency.

09-018.r: Shrillness depends on frequency; frequency and wavelength are inversely related (v = frequency × wavelength), so book answers wavelength: shorter wavelength → shriller sound.
09-018.t: Don't confuse: loudness depends on amplitude; shrillness (pitch) on frequency/wavelength.

09-019.r: No atmosphere (vacuum) on the Moon → no medium for sound, so astronauts cannot hear each other directly.

09-021.r: Both false: a shorter flute gives higher frequency (shorter wavelength); in solids like rocks sound travels as both longitudinal and transverse waves, not longitudinal only.

09-022.r: Both true: P waves reach a seismograph before S waves; P waves → particles vibrate along the direction of travel; S waves → at right angles (up and down).

09-023.r: Ultrasonic waves (above 20,000 Hz) can kill insects, clean clothes, treat diseases, control automatic doors, detect submarines and find sea depth (all correct).

09-025.r: Human audible range → 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
09-025.h: Below 20 Hz infrasonic; 20–20,000 Hz audible; above 20,000 Hz ultrasonic.

09-026.r: All three false: audible range is 20 Hz–20 kHz (not 10 kHz); ultrasound is above 20 kHz; earthquakes produce infrasound (below 20 Hz) before main shocks.

09-027.r: Sonography (ultrasonography) uses ultrasonic waves; used to check growth of the foetus in the womb and the mother's health.

09-029.r: Bats emit ultrasonic sounds and use the returning echoes to fly and catch prey in the dark → echolocation.

09-030.r: Correct: heart vibrates at infrasonic; Mach number compares an object's speed with sound's speed; ultrasonic > 20,000 Hz. Wrong: sound is fastest in solids, not gases.

09-031.r: Stethoscope → heartbeat sound reaches the doctor's ears by multiple reflection of sound inside its tube.

09-032.r: Supersonic jets (faster than sound) fly at stratosphere height and emit nitrogen oxide, which depletes the ozone layer.

09-033.r: Speed of sound rises with temperature; at 15 km altitude it is colder, so sound (and Mach 1) is slower than at sea level (A false, R true).

09-034.r: Decibel (dB) measures the intensity (sound-pressure level) of sound/noise in the atmosphere.

09-037.r: Normal conversation → about 30–60 dB (answer: about 30 dB); whisper 15–20 dB; machine shop 100–110 dB; jet plane 140–150 dB.

09-039.r: Rustling of tree leaves → about 20 dB; decibel = 1/10 bel, named after Alexander Graham Bell.

09-040.r: WHO safe noise level for a city → 45 dB.

09-041.r: Noise Rules 2000, day/night dB: silent zone 50/40, residential 55/45, commercial 65/55, industrial 75/70 (answer pairs industrial with 70).

09-042.r: Tolerable noise limit for humans → about 85 dB (book: continuous 80 dB is harmful, 90 dB is the maximum); normal conversation 30–60 dB; 50 dB can wake a sleeper.

09-043.r: Sound above 80 dB → hazardous noise pollution; noise is measured in decibels.

09-045.r: Optimum sound level for humans → about 60 dB (normal conversation); above 80 dB can damage ear cells.

09-046.r: Loudness depends on amplitude: larger amplitude → more energy → louder sound.

09-047.r: Boy hears the blow twice: sound reaches first through the steel rail (faster) and then through air.

09-048.r: Only I true: sound slows from solid to gas. False: lower temperature raises speed (it lowers it); sound is slower in aluminium than glass (it is slower in glass).

09-049.r: Sound passing into another medium → frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change (amplitude also falls with distance).

09-050.r: Sitarist adjusting tension tunes the string's frequency to match other instruments; string frequency depends on length, diameter, density and tension.

09-051.r: Same note on sitar and flute is told apart by quality (timbre) only; it separates sounds of equal pitch and loudness.

09-052.r: Basic (smallest) unit of sound in a language → phoneme; it can change meaning but has no meaning by itself.

09-053.r: Reverberation (felt in large churches and buildings) → multiple reflections from walls, roof and ground (A and R true, R explains A).

09-054.r: Diatonic scale has eight notes (octave; last:first = 2:1), not seven. If Sa = 256 Hz, Ni = 480 Hz and upper Sa = 512 Hz (both false).
09-054.h: Octave = eight notes; upper Sa is double the lower Sa.

09-055.r: TV signals cannot be received beyond a certain distance because Earth's surface is curved.

09-056.r: Switching on a (modern) TV → audio and video start together (audio synchronizer); old sets showed video late because of warm-up time.

09-057.r: TV broadcast: picture (video) signals → amplitude modulation; sound (audio) signals → frequency modulation.
09-057.t: Don't swap them: TV picture → AM, TV sound → FM.

09-058.r: TV audio signals are sent by frequency modulation (FM): larger bandwidth, little noise or interference.

10-001.r: Current density → current per unit cross-section area (A/m²); a vector quantity, direction of positive charge motion.

10-002.r: Dielectric constant (relative permittivity) → dimensionless, M⁰L⁰T⁰; measures a material's ability to store electrical energy.

10-003.r: Charge e moving through potential difference V gains energy E = eV joules (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

10-004.r: 100 W bulb × 10 hours = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh = 1 unit; at Rs 5 per unit → Rs 5.

10-006.r: One 200 W bulb for 24 h = 200 × 24 ÷ 1000 = 4.8 units; 15 bulbs → 15 × 4.8 = 72 units.

10-007.r: One 100 W bulb for twenty hours = 2 kWh = 2 units; five bulbs → 2 × 5 = 10 units.

10-008.r: 1 kWh = 1000 J/s × 3600 s = 36 lakh joules = 3.6 million J (option a).

10-009.r: 100 W bulb for 4 hours = 400 Wh = 0.4 kWh = 0.4 unit.

10-010.r: Electricity bill is based on energy in kilowatt hour (watt-based; 1 unit = 1000 W for 1 hour), not volt, ohm or ampere.

10-011.r: Units = watt × hour ÷ 1000: 60 W × 5 h × 30 days ÷ 1000 = 9 units.

10-012.r: 1 unit = 1 kWh = 1000 J/s × 3600 s = 3,600,000 J; 250 units = 900 million joules (option c).

10-013.r: Electric power P = VI = I²R = V²/R (watt); IR² (I × R²) is not a power formula.

10-014.r: Power P = VI = 220 V × 0.5 A = 110 W.

10-015.r: Ohm's law: resistance R = V/I (voltage ÷ current), at constant temperature.

10-016.r: At the same voltage, P = V²/R → power ∝ 1/R; so the dim bulb has larger resistance, the bright bulb smaller.

10-018.r: Two identical bulbs glow brighter in parallel: each gets full circuit voltage (P = V²/R); in series their resistances add up.

10-020.r: Colour code: brown 1, green 5, black 0 (multiplier 1) → 15 Ω; current I = V/R = 15 V ÷ 15 Ω = 1 A.

10-021.r: Capacitive reactance X = 1/(2πfC) → inversely proportional to frequency; inductive reactance X = 2πfL → directly proportional.
10-021.t: Don't confuse capacitor (X ∝ 1/f) with inductor (X ∝ f).

10-022.r: Dynamo (generator) does not create charge; it is a converter of energy → mechanical rotation into electric current (Faraday's law).

10-023.r: Dynamo → converts mechanical energy into electrical energy (gives direct current via a commutator); turbines and dynamos turn mechanical energy into electricity.

10-026.r: Book: when electrical energy is converted into motion, there is no heat loss.
10-026.c: Real motors always lose some energy as heat; the book's answer 'no heat loss' is the ideal case.

10-027.r: Electric motor → converts electrical energy into mechanical energy (rotating coils driven by magnetic force).
10-027.t: Don't confuse motor (electrical → mechanical) with dynamo (mechanical → electrical).

10-029.r: Book's two answers: dynamo and electric motor both work on electromagnetic induction (dynamo: mechanical → electrical; motor: electrical → mechanical).

10-030.r: Battery → converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy; parts: positive electrode, negative electrode, electrolyte.

10-031.r: Electric motors at low voltage burn out because they draw more current (current inversely proportional to voltage).

10-032.r: Faraday constant F → electric charge per mole of electrons; a universal constant, F = 96485.332123 C/mol.

10-033.r: Car battery: about 12 V (six 2 V cells in series); capacity in ampere-hour. Electrolyte is about 35% sulphuric acid (not HCl); electrodes lead and lead dioxide (not copper).

10-034.r: Ni-Cd (rechargeable) battery: nickel oxide hydroxide and cadmium electrodes, potassium hydroxide electrolyte; used in calculators, cordless appliances, transistors (all).

10-035.r: Electric bulb filament → tungsten; tungsten was first isolated in 1783 by Juan Jose and Fausto Elhuyar.

10-038.r: Ordinary bulb has short life: filament wire not uniform, bulb cannot be fully evacuated, supporting wires melt at high temperature (all three).

10-039.r: Lit bulb's tungsten filament → about 2000–2500°C (book: up to 1500–2500°C); bulbs turn only 5–10% of electric energy into light.

10-040.r: Lightning can burn a tree because it carries a huge amount of electrical energy (electric discharge between clouds and ground).

10-041.r: Lightning conductor: metal rod on top of a building, wired to the ground, carries the charge to earth instead of through the structure (A and R true, R explains A).

10-042.r: Three-pin plug: longest pin → earth (ground) terminal; it connects first and disconnects last; earthing is for safety.

10-044.r: No current flows between two charged bodies at the same potential; current needs a potential difference.

10-045.r: Fuse → safety device in series; its thin wire melts on overload or short circuit and breaks the circuit, protecting appliances.

10-046.r: Fuse wire must have a low melting point; fuse works on the heating effect of electric current and melts when current exceeds a limit.

10-048.r: Fuse wire → high resistance and low melting point.
10-048.h: Fuse: high R, low melt; it heats fast and melts fast.

10-050.r: Fuse wire: usually tin–lead alloy (about 63% tin, 37% lead), melting point about 183°C, far lower than copper (1085°C) and aluminium; A true, R false.

10-051.r: Short circuit → resistance falls near zero, so current rises very high (I = V/R), causing heat and fire risk.

10-052.r: Halogen lamp → tungsten filament inside a bulb of halogen gas (iodine or bromine), giving white light. The book's 'alloy of tungsten and sodium' is wrong.
10-052.c: A halogen lamp has a plain tungsten filament in a bulb filled with halogen gas (iodine or bromine) and gives white light, so 'tungsten and sodium' is wrong; (a) tungsten and iodine is the usual answer.

10-053.r: Wire heats up because moving electrons collide with the conductor's atoms and pass on energy (A true); not because metal atoms collide with each other (R false).

10-054.r: Domestic wiring → parallel connection: if one bulb or branch is removed, current still flows in other branches and they keep working.
10-054.c: The book says each parallel branch gets equal current; in fact each branch gets the same voltage, and current depends on the appliance.

10-055.r: House wiring colour code: live → red, neutral → black, earth → green.
10-055.h: Red = live danger; Black = neutral; Green = ground (earth).

10-056.r: Dry human body resistance → about 10,000 ohm (option b), may reach 100,000 ohm; wet or broken skin can drop it to 1000 ohm or less.

10-057.r: CFL → Compact Fluorescent Lamp; uses about 75% less energy than traditional bulbs.

10-058.r: LED works on electroluminescence: a semiconductor emits light when current passes (electrons and holes recombine, releasing photons).

10-059.r: LED lamps last longer than CFLs (A) because they use less energy (R explains A); LED uses gallium arsenide to emit light.

10-060.r: CFL → mercury vapour + phosphor; LED → semiconductor. CFL is less efficient and shorter-lived (about 6000–15,000 hours), so 'CFL lasts longer' is false.
